blocks.text: 1. Skip-gram

blocks.alt: A target word goes through Skip-gram to predict context words

blocks.text: CBOW, the previous topic, predicted a single target word from its surrounding context. Skip-gram is Word2Vec's other variant, predicting context from a single word instead, explored throughout this topic.
It uses the genuinely reverse direction: one word genuinely predicting several surrounding context words, a genuinely direct mirror of the direction already covered in the previous topic.
2. Recapping The Preview

This connects back to two Word2Vec architectures, already covered in Word2Vec. Skip-gram was genuinely introduced there as the second of two Word2Vec variants, briefly described in that earlier topic.
This topic genuinely gives it the complete, dedicated treatment already promised, exploring every detail already hinted at generally in that earlier topic.
3. The Reversed Direction

blocks.alt: A target word predicts context words

blocks.text: Skip-gram's genuinely defining direction connects back to the prediction direction, already covered in CBOW. Given a genuinely single target word, genuinely predict each of its surrounding context words.
This is the exact genuinely reversed direction from CBOW's own approach already covered there, choosing genuinely word-to-context as its own particular direction instead.

blocks.text: 4. Multiple Predictions Per Target Word

blocks.alt: A target word predicts context word 1 and context word 2

blocks.text: This connects back to the context window, already covered in Word2Vec. Skip-gram genuinely makes one separate prediction for every single context position, already covered there as the window's own size.
This happens rather than CBOW's own single, combined prediction already covered in the previous topic, a genuinely important structural difference explored throughout the rest of this topic.
5. Why Skip-gram Is Genuinely More Computationally Intensive

blocks.alt: Skip-gram makes multiple predictions while CBOW makes one

blocks.text: This connects back to why CBOW is genuinely less computationally intensive, already covered in CBOW. Skip-gram genuinely makes multiple separate predictions per target word instead of just one.
This directly reverses the efficiency advantage already covered for CBOW in the previous topic, a genuinely real, honest tradeoff explored throughout the rest of this topic.
6. Skip-gram Genuinely Suits Rare Words

blocks.alt: Skip-gram works well for rare words

blocks.text: This connects back to CBOW genuinely suits frequent words, already covered in CBOW. Skip-gram genuinely treats every context word as its own genuinely separate training example, unlike CBOW's own averaging already covered there.

This makes it genuinely especially effective for learning representations of genuinely rare, uncommon words, a genuinely direct, complementary strength to CBOW's own genuine focus already covered in the previous topic.

blocks.content: This complementary strength, already covered in this topic, directly explains why CBOW and Skip-gram, both already covered, remain two genuinely valid, distinct choices depending on the specific vocabulary characteristics of a given task.

blocks.text: 7. CBOW Versus Skip-gram, Directly Compared

blocks.alt: CBOW maps context to word while Skip-gram maps word to context

blocks.text: This connects back to the prediction direction, already covered in this topic and CBOW. CBOW genuinely predicts one word from several; Skip-gram genuinely predicts several words from one.

These are two genuinely opposite, complementary directions built from the exact same underlying Word2Vec idea, already covered in that earlier topic, each with its own genuinely distinctive strengths already covered throughout this topic.

blocks.text: 8. Recapping The Role Of Negative Sampling
This connects back to a preview of negative sampling, already covered in Word2Vec. Skip-gram genuinely benefits especially strongly from negative sampling, already covered there.

This holds since it genuinely makes considerably more individual predictions per target word than CBOW does, already covered earlier in this topic, making that efficiency technique genuinely especially valuable here.
9. Recognizing When Skip-gram Is Genuinely The Right Variant

blocks.alt: Needing better rare word vectors points toward Skip-gram

blocks.text: This connects back to genuinely needing strong representations of genuinely rare, uncommon words, already covered in this topic. Skip-gram, already covered in this topic, directly delivers exactly that strength.

This connects back to CBOW, already covered, favoring genuinely faster training with frequent words instead. Skip-gram, already covered, remains the genuinely better choice when rare-word quality matters more.
10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates Skip-gram's own multiple-prediction structure, contrasting it directly with CBOW's own single-prediction structure already covered in the previous topic.

code.content:
sentence = ["the", "quick", "brown", "fox", "jumps"]
window_size = 2  # already covered as the context window in Word2Vec

target_index = 2  # "brown" is the target word, already covered as the reversed direction in this topic
context_start = max(0, target_index - window_size)
context_end = min(len(sentence), target_index + window_size + 1)
context_words = [sentence[j] for j in range(context_start, context_end) if j != target_index]

# already covered as multiple predictions per target word in this topic
skip_gram_pairs = [(sentence[target_index], context_word) for context_word in context_words]

print(f"Target word: '{sentence[target_index]}'")
print("Skip-gram training pairs (already covered as multiple predictions per target word in this topic):")
for target, context in skip_gram_pairs:
    print(f"  Predict '{context}' from '{target}'")

print(f"\nTotal separate predictions from this one target word: {len(skip_gram_pairs)}")
print("Compare this to CBOW's own single, combined prediction from all context words at once, already covered in the previous topic")

blocks.content: Running this example shows one single target word producing multiple separate training predictions, exactly the multiple-predictions structure already covered in this topic, in direct contrast with CBOW's own single, combined prediction.

blocks.text: 11. Embeddings: Progress Recap

items: Skip-gram predicts each surrounding context word from a single target word.
This reverses CBOW's own direction, which predicts a target word from its context.
It makes one separate prediction for every single context position.
This makes Skip-gram more computationally intensive than CBOW's own single, combined prediction.
Treating every context word separately makes Skip-gram especially effective for rare, uncommon words.
CBOW and Skip-gram represent two opposite, complementary directions of the same underlying idea.
Skip-gram benefits especially strongly from negative sampling, given its many individual predictions.
It is the better choice when rare-word representation quality matters more than training speed.
